sentences.text: Magistrate, 46th Court, Mazgaon, Mumbai, thereby, the Respondents/Original Accused Nos.1 to 3 have been acquitted of the charge of the offences punishable under Sections 7 (i) read with Section 2 (ia) (a) punishable under Section 16 (1) (a)(ii), Section 7 (i) read with Section 2 (ia) (m) punishable under section 16 (1) (a) (i) read with Section 17 of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

(Hereinafter the Respondents are being referred to by their status in the trial i.e., A1 to A3).
2) Heard Ms. Tendulkar, the learned APP for the Appellant- State and Mr. Kanal, the learned Advocate for accused Nos. 1 and 3.
Perused the record.

2.1) Record indicates that as per the Order dated 12/07/2016 the Appeal has been dismissed against Respondent No.2 for not taking necessary steps within the stipulated time to serve the said Respondent.
Thereafter, no steps were taken by the Appellant to restore the Appeal against Respondent No.2.

3) The story of the prosecution is as under :
3.1) As alleged, A1 was stocking the goods, i.e., Super Refined Sunflower Oil on behalf of his company M/s.Reliable Carrier Private Limited, Anant Ganpat Pawar Cross Lane No.2, Byculla (E), Mumbai - 27.

Said Oil was being manufactured by A3 (M/s. I.T.C. Agro Tech Limited) for which A2 (Mr.Hidayatulla) was nominee.
 H.C. SHIV 42.app124.2000.doc 3.2)
That, Mr. A. N. Rana (PW No.3) was appointed as a Food Inspector for the Greater Mumbai, by the Government of Maharashtra as per the Gazette dated 20/11/1984.
On 04/08/1994, around 4.00 PM, PW3 visited the premises of M/s.Reliable Carrier Private Limited.
A1 was present in the said premises and working there as a Godown Keeper.

PW3 disclosed his identity to A1 and inspected the premises, during which PW3 found that A1 had stocked there for sale 'I.T.C. Sundrop brand Super Refined Sunflower Oil', in the company packed plastic bottles of one liter capacity.

sentences.text: PW3 demanded and purchased 450 gm of I.T.C. Sundrop brand Super Refined Sunflower Oil from a packed plastic bottle and paid Rs.25/- in cash to A1 and obtained a receipt.
At the same time, PW3 issued Form No.VI of P.F.A. Act to the accused intimating him that the sample was purchased for chemical analysis.
PW3 also issued the notice under Section 14 (A) and called upon A1 to disclose the name and address of the supplier.
Thereafter PW3 stirred the Oil, divided it in three equal parts and filled each part separately in a dry, clean and empty glass bottle.
Each bottle was stoppered securely and sealed.
The label bearing the relevant particulars of the L.H.A. was pasted on each of the bottles.
Each sample bottle was separately wrapped in appropriate brown paper and sealed.

The paper slip bearing signature of the L.H.A. and AHO-I of Greater Bombay was pasted over it in a H.C. SHIV 42.app124.2000.doc proper manner and tide The State Of Maharashtra vs Shri. Parminder Singh K. Arora on 12 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/122705741/
2 with a strong twine.

sentences.text: Thereafter each sample was signed by A1 and sealed by PW3, as required in law.
Lastly, PW3 recorded a Panchanama of the aforesaid entire action.
3.3) On 05/08/1994, PW3 sent one sealed sample alongwith copy of memorandum in Form No.VII in a sealed packet to the Public Analyst, Dadar, Mumbai along with a forwarding letter.
On the same day, he sent to the Public Analyst the specimen seal impression of the seal used for sealing the samples, alongwith a copy of Form No.VII, in a sealed packet.
On the same day PW3 sent the remaining two samples and the copies of the Form No.VII to L.H.A. and AHO-I of Greater Bombay, alongwith a forwarding letter.
PW3 also sent separate specimen seal impression to L.H.A. and AHO-I of Greater Bombay, which seal he used to seal the sample.

3.4) On 19/09/1994 PW3 received the report of the Public Analyst through the L.H.A. disclosing that the Oil sample was found adulterated as it was not in conformity with the standards vide Section 2 (ia) (m) read with Rule 5 (A).17.22 of the P.F.A. Act and the Rules thereunder.

Thereafter,
PW3 collected necessary documentary information and sent entire material alongwith Proforma-A to the Joint Commissioner, F.D.A. to get the consent under Section 20 of the P.F.A. Act.
Subsequently, PW3 was transferred, so, he handed over the charge to P.M. Waghmare, Food Inspector from whom PW2- H.C. SHIV 42.app124.2000.doc Mr.S. N. Mane, Food Inspector received the charge of PW3.
In due course, PW2 received the consent of the Joint Commissioner on 31/07/1995 and then he filed the complaint on 21/08/1995.
4) In response to the process, the accused appeared in the case.
The particulars of the offence were read-over and explained to the accused by the trial Court.
The accused pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried.
5) It was the defence of the accused that A1 was only the clearing and forwarding agent.
Neither A1 was stocking the goods for sale nor selling the same in his premises, therefore, he was no way concerned with the alleged offence.
It was the case of A2 and A3 that PW3 was not appointed as contemplated under Section 9 of the P.F.A. Act.
Therefore, the action of drawing the samples was unauthorised.

There was no proper sampling, because though the packed oil bottles were available,
the same were not taken as sample and sent in the same condition for the analysis.
The analysis of the sample was not properly done.
However, the A2 and A3 have been implicated in this case on the strength of the incorrect and fake report of analysis.

6) In support of its case the prosecution examined in all five witnesses, who are :-
(1) Ravindra Chitnis (PW No.1) - the L.H.A. Clerk, who filed on record the documents at Ex.P-1 to Ex.P-10.
H.C. SHIV 42.app124.2000.doc (2) S.N. Mane, Food Inspector (PW.No.2) - He received the charge from Food Inspector Mr.Waghmare and the consent order of the Joint Commissioner - F.D.A. and then filed the complaint.

Akkalwar (PW.No.5) - the Assistant Chemist who analysed the sample under the supervision of PW.No.4, in the laboratory at Dadar, and also prepared the notes."
7) Ms. Tendulkar, the learned APP submitted that the accused did not dispute that A1 was present at the godown when PW3 visited and inspected there.
It is also not disputed that PW3 purchased the Oil bottle and drew samples from it.

She submitted that, there is sufficient evidence by the prosecution that PW3 sealed the samples in accordance with the procedure in law and thereafter, the relevant sample was analysed by PW4 And PW5.
Said Analyses revealed that the subject Oil was adulterated, yet, the accused persons stored that Oil with an intent to sell the same in the open market.
As such, the offences stated in the charge were proved.

However,
the trial Court acquitted the accused persons for technical reasons.

As such, H.C.
SHIV 42.app124.2000.doc the impugned Judgment and Order is against the evidence on record and the applicable law, therefore, the same be set aside and the accused may be convicted and sentenced.
8) Mr. Kanal, the learned Advocate for the accused, on the other hand, submitted that the prosecution failed to prove the sanction as required by Section 20 of the Act,
hence , the proceeding was vitiated.
This aspect was conceded by the prosecution.

He submitted that the Sunflower oil bottles of one litre each were in a sealed and packed condition, nevertheless, the Food Inspector took the samples from one such bottle instead of taking three bottles as samples.

This practice is against the provisions of Rule 22-A of the Food Adulteration Rules, which provides that, where food is sold or stocked for sale or for distribution in sealed containers having identical label declaration, the contents of one or more of such containers as may be required to satisfy the quantity prescribed in Rule 22 shall be treated to be a part of the sample.
He submitted that even if it is accepted that the samples were properly taken and analysed, yet, the prosecution failed to prove that the subject Oil was adulterated.
As such, the acquittal of the accused persons by the trial Court is lawful and need not be upset.

To support his submissions, Mr. Kanal cited the following decisions:
 H.C. SHIV 42.app124.2000.doc  i) State of Maharashtra V/s. R.A.Chandavarkar & Others1

sentences.text: the evidence on record

. On such exercise, I found that the accused party has not disputed that PW3 visited the godown premises of A1 on 04/08/1994, and purchased for price the I.T.C. Sundrop Super refined Sunflower Oil packed in 1 litter plastic bottle, manufactured by I.T.C. Agro-Tech Limited, Secunderabad, Andhra Pradesh;
that, he took 450 gm of the Oil from it for the sampling purpose; that, he prepared the three samples of the said Oil and completed the procedure, as contemplated in law.

10) However, In the cross-examination, PW3 admitted that after his second training was over on 25/04/1988, there was notification of the Government thereby appointing him as the Food Inspector for the locality of Greater Mumbai as provided by Sec.9 of the P.F.A. Act.
Therefore, the trial Court observed and held that, the notification prior to the second training of PW3 will not validate his posting as a Food Inspector U/sec.9 of the P.F.A. Act.

This serious infirmity goes to the root of the case and therefore raised the question 1 All MR (Cri.) 773 (Bombay) 2 1999 (1) FAC 18 H.C. SHIV 42.app124.2000.doc as to whether PW3 was competent to draw the Oil sample on 04/08/1994 or not.

11) The evidence of PW3 indicates that, he was transferred from Mumbai in May 1995, therefore, he orally handed-over the charge to Food Inspector Mr. Waghmare and later on, Mr. Waghmare orally handed-over the charge to PW2, who filed the complaint.
The trial Court observed that, though there was notification dated 03/09/93 (Ex.P-11), by that notification PW2 was posted at Usmanabad and not in Mumbai.
There is another departmental Order dated 24/04/95 (Ex.P-12), signed by the commissioner, F.D.A., by which PW2 was transferred from Usmanabad to Mumbai.
However, PW2 admitted that this transfer Order was not notified in the Gazette.

11.1) The aforesaid background made the trial Court to observe that, as per Sec.9 of the P.F.A. Act, the State Government by way of notification in official gazette has to appoint the Food Inspector for a particular area.
When the appointment of Food Inspector is directed by the statute in particular manner, it must be done in that manner and not otherwise.
Therefore, the postings as contemplated U/sec.9 of the P.F.A. Act is a statutory posting and not an administrative posting.
To fortify this observations, the trial Court relied upon the decision in the case of R.A.Chandavarkar & Others (supra).
H.C. SHIV 42.app124.2000.doc 12)
It is fact that the one litre Oil, which PW3 purchased for the sake of this case, was in the sealed and packed plastic bottle.
PW3 broke open the seal of the bottle and collected the 450 gms of Oil in the steel utensil and then divided that portion into three parts/samples.
However, he did not retain the remaining Oil in the bottle.
PW3 candidly admitted that he could have taken as samples three sealed bottles of one litre each, however, he has not, for the best reason known to him.

PW3 denied that because of the opening of the plastic bottle the The State Of Maharashtra vs Shri. Parminder Singh K. Arora on 12 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/122705741/
5 identity of the sample was destroyed.

sentences.text: Therefore, the trial Court has rightly observed that when separate three sealed Oil bottles were available, it was appreciable to take the sample in the same condition and to send it for analysis so as to draw the correct conclusion at the time of analysis.
As such, there is infirmity in respect of drawing an appropriate sample of the Oil in question.

13) Mr. Kanal, the learned Advocate for the Respondents pointed the Public Analyst's Report (Exh.P-6) and submitted that the B.R. Reading was certified as 57.0 against the prescribed standard of 57.1.
The alleged failure was 0.1 Unit under Rule A.17.22.
The mandatory scientific procedure demands that, the B.R. Apparatus must necessarily be standardised and corrected to zero error before commencement of the test.
The apparatus must be mandatorily standardised with standard liquid "1-Bromnapthalin".
However, PW4 H.C. SHIV 42.app124.2000.doc admitted that said standard liquid was not available in his laboratory.
That apart, the apparatus was standardised with distilled water.
Thus the mandatory requirement was ignored.
The B.R. apparatus used in the process, was more than 30 years old.
PW4 admitted that his laboratory did not have the manufacturer's manual and the standard liquid, when the test was performed.
He admitted that in his entire career he has never seen the standard liquid.
Further he admitted that if the instrument is not standardised and corrected for zero error, the reading would be incorrect and unreliable.
In view of this evidence, the trial Court held that the conclusion drawn by PW4 after the alleged analysis cannot be safely accepted.
14) About Saponification Value as per I.S. Standard, the trial Court noted that the equation of S.V. is :-
Saponification Value = 56.1 (B-S) N Where - B = Volume in m.l. of standard Hydrochloric Acid required for the blank.
S = Volume in m.l. standard Hydrochloric Acid required for the sample.
N = Normality of the standard Hydrochloric Acid.
W = Weight in gms. of the material taken for the test.

In this regard, PW4 admitted that in the Second determination, the weight of the sample taken for SV was higher than the first one,
namely 2.2767 gms. against 2.2053 gms.

As the weight of the sample in the 2nd determination was admittedly higher than the first one the reading of 'S' in the Second determination must necessarily be higher than '9.4', but it was actually lower,
i.e., 8.9.
Thus, it appeared that as per the report and protocols SV was 198.4 which was 4.4 units higher than the prescribed range of 181 - 194.
However, the trial Court held that, incorrect analysis was responsible for the said increase.

sentences.text: The evidence indicates that, the Iodine Value was calculated as per WIJ's method.
However, it was not mentioned in the P.A. Report.
PW4 admitted that there was deviation and departure about the Iodine Value because he used Iodine trichloride instead of Iodine monochloride.
Likewise, he used chloroform solvent instead of Carbon tetrachloride.

About I.V. Test, the evidence of PW4 and his Assistant PW5 indicate that all the nine reagents were prepared on 24/8/1994 and on the same day,
I.V. Test was performed twice and that too, simultaneously.
Therefore the trial Court observed that, according to I.S. Standard, prior to standardisation, the Sodium Thiosulphate solution is to be stored for about two weeks for the purpose of stabilization.
But in this case it was not stored for two H.C. SHIV 42.app124.2000.doc weeks and thus there was no certainty of the proper conclusion about the I.V. Test.
In the backdrop, the trial Court held that the Public Analyst's report was not in conformity with the standards and hence, refused to rely upon the same.
16) The trial Court noted that, in the present case the prosecution could not prove the consent accorded under Section 20 of the Act, because his predecessor had closed the evidence.
Even if the consent was proved, the infirmities found in respect of drawing the sample and in the analysis thereof eroded the way to prove the guilt of the accused.
17) In view of the above discussion, I hold that the impugned Judgment and Order of the acquittal is based on appreciating the prosecution evidence in its correct perspective.
Therefore, it does not require any interference by this Court.

As a result,
the Appeal is liable to be dismissed.

17.1) Hence, following Order is passed :-
i) Appeal is dismissed against Respondent Nos.1 and 3.
ii) R & P shall be immediately returned to the trial Court.

(SHYAM C. CHANDAK, J.)
